questions.question_text:
An account begins with $\$8000$ and receives regular deposits of $\$500$ at the end of each year for $6\text{ years}$ at $5\%$ p.a. compounded annually.
Find the future value of the account to the nearest cent.

options.why: Calculated compound interest on the lump sum alone without adding the annuity series.
Added the initial deposit of $\$8000$ and uncompounded regular deposits totalling $\$3000$, without calculating compound interest.
Subtracted the annuity series from the compounded lump sum instead of adding it.

questions.solution_text:
The deposits form $S=500+500(1.05)+\cdots+500(1.05)^5$, with $6$ terms and common ratio $1.05$.
$FV=8000(1.05)^6+\dfrac{500(1.05^6-1)}{0.05}=\$14\,121.72$.
Evaluate the whole expression before rounding. The principal-only value is $\$10\,720.77$ and subtracting the series instead gives $\$7319.81$, so only the first option includes both components correctly.

questions.question_text:
A retirement account starts with $\$80\,000$ earning $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
At the end of each month, $\$900$ is withdrawn.
Calculate the balance remaining in the account after $5\text{ years}$, to the nearest cent.

options.why: Added the withdrawal series to the compounded principal instead of subtracting it.
Subtracted uncompounded withdrawals totalling $\$54\,000$ from the initial $\$80\,000$, ignoring interest.
Incorrectly treated the monthly withdrawals as one withdrawal of $\$10\,800$ at each year-end and compounded annually at $6\%$.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.06/12=0.005$, $n=60$.
The withdrawals form $900+900(1.005)+\cdots+900(1.005)^{59}$, with common ratio $1.005$ and $60$ terms.
$A_{60}=80000(1.005)^{60}-\dfrac{900(1.005^{60}-1)}{0.005}$.
The balance to cents is $\$45\,114.98$.
It is positive, so all $60$ withdrawals are affordable. The distractors respectively add withdrawals, ignore interest, or move the monthly cashflows to year-end; none equals the correct balance.

questions.question_text:
An investor deposits $\$15\,000$ initially and adds $\$300$ at the end of each month for $3\text{ years}$ into an account earning $7.2\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
Find the final balance to the nearest cent.

options.why: Compounded the initial $\$15\,000$ but omitted the monthly contributions.
Added the initial $\$15\,000$ to $36$ uncompounded deposits of $\$300$, ignoring interest.
Subtracted the contribution series from the compounded lump sum instead of adding it.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.072/12=0.006$, $n=36$.
The deposits form $300+300(1.006)+\cdots+300(1.006)^{35}$, with $36$ terms and common ratio $1.006$.
$FV=15000(1.006)^{36}+\dfrac{300(1.006^{36}-1)}{0.006}$.
The final balance to cents is $\$30\,619.60$.
Round only the final sum. The correct balance exceeds both principal-only compounding and uncompounded total deposits; subtraction gives a smaller value, so exactly one option is correct.

questions.question_text:
A person wants to invest a single lump sum $PV$ into an account earning $4.8\%$ p.a. compounded monthly in order to withdraw $\$1500$ at the end of each month for $8\text{ years}$ ($n=96$), leaving a balance of $\$0$.
Find the required lump sum $PV$ to the nearest cent.

options.why: Multiplied $\$1500$ by $96$ months without accounting for interest earned during drawdown.
Calculated the future value of the withdrawals but omitted division by the principal's growth factor.
Discounted the simple total of $\$144\,000$ as though all withdrawals occurred at the final date.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.004$, $n=96$.
The withdrawals form $1500+1500(1.004)+\cdots+1500(1.004)^{95}$, with common ratio $1.004$ and $96$ terms.
$0=PV(1.004)^{96}-\dfrac{1500(1.004^{96}-1)}{0.004}$.
$PV=\dfrac{1500(1.004^{96}-1)}{0.004(1.004)^{96}}$.
The principal to cents is $\$119\,380.00$.
Substitution of the unrounded principal gives exactly zero. The correct principal is below the uncompounded total but above that total discounted wholly from month $96$; the future-value distractor is larger than the uncompounded total, so all four options differ.

questions.question_text:
A fund begins with $\$40\,000$ and earns $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
If $\$1000$ is withdrawn at the end of each month, how many complete withdrawals of $\$1000$ can be made in full?

options.why: Rounded the zero-balance solution up. The balance immediately after withdrawal $44$ is about $\$737$; it grows by a factor of $1.005$ before withdrawal $45$, but remains below $\$1000$.
Divided $\$40\,000$ by $\$1000$ without accounting for interest earned during the drawdown period.
Used $n=1.25/0.005=250$ instead of taking logarithms of $(1.005)^n=1.25$.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.06/12=0.005$.
The withdrawals form $1000+1000(1.005)+\cdots+1000(1.005)^{n-1}$, with common ratio $1.005$.
$0=40000(1.005)^n-\dfrac{1000(1.005^n-1)}{0.005}$.
$160000(1.005)^n=200000$, so $(1.005)^n=1.25$.
$n=\dfrac{\ln1.25}{\ln1.005}\approx44.74$.
The balance after $44$ full withdrawals is positive. Before withdrawal $45$, the available amount is $[200000-160000(1.005)^{44}](1.005)<1000$.
Therefore exactly $44$ full withdrawals can be made; month $45$ allows only a partial withdrawal. The other options respectively round up, ignore interest, or replace the logarithmic calculation with division.

questions.question_text:
A company sets up an equipment maintenance fund with an initial $\$60\,000$ earning $5.4\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
At the end of each month, $\$1200$ is withdrawn for servicing.
Calculate the balance of the fund after $4\text{ years}$, to the nearest cent.

options.why: Added the withdrawal series to the compounded principal instead of subtracting it.
Subtracted $48$ uncompounded withdrawals of $\$1200$ from $\$60\,000$, ignoring interest.
Compounded the initial deposit but omitted the monthly withdrawals.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.054/12=0.0045$, $n=48$.
The withdrawals form $1200+1200(1.0045)+\cdots+1200(1.0045)^{47}$, with $48$ terms and common ratio $1.0045$.
$A_{48}=60000(1.0045)^{48}-\dfrac{1200(1.0045^{48}-1)}{0.0045}$.
The balance to cents is $\$10\,296.43$.
It is positive, so all $48$ withdrawals are affordable. Interest makes this balance greater than $\$2400$, but subtracting withdrawals makes it smaller than principal-only compounding; adding withdrawals gives an even larger result. Exactly one option is correct.

questions.question_text:
A retiree wants to withdraw $\$2200$ at the end of each month for $15\text{ years}$ from a fund earning $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly, leaving a balance of $\$0$ immediately after the final withdrawal.
Find the required initial lump sum to the nearest cent.

options.why: Multiplied $180$ withdrawals by $\$2200$ without accounting for interest earned by the remaining fund.
Used the future value of the withdrawal series as the initial deposit, omitting division by $(1.005)^{180}$.
Discounted all $\$396\,000$ from the final month instead of accounting for the separate monthly withdrawal dates.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.06/12=0.005$, $n=15\times12=180$.
The withdrawals form $2200+2200(1.005)+\cdots+2200(1.005)^{179}$, with $180$ terms and common ratio $1.005$.
$0=P(1.005)^{180}-\dfrac{2200(1.005^{180}-1)}{0.005}$.
$P=\dfrac{2200(1.005^{180}-1)}{0.005(1.005)^{180}}$.
The required deposit to cents is $\$260\,707.73$.
The unrounded deposit gives exact exhaustion after withdrawal $180$; rounding the deposit can leave a small rounding difference. The correct present value lies between the final-date discounted total and the uncompounded total, while the future-value distractor exceeds the total, so exactly one option is correct.

questions.question_text:
A scholarship fund starts with $\$120\,000$ earning $4.8\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
If $\$1400$ is withdrawn at the end of each month, how many complete withdrawals of $\$1400$ can be made in full?

options.why: Rounded the zero-balance solution up even though withdrawal $105$ can only be partial.
Ignored interest and rounded down $120000/1400$.
Used the annual growth factor $1.048$ instead of the monthly growth factor $1.004$ only in the logarithm denominator, calculating $\ln(35/23)/\ln(1.048)$ and rounding down.

questions.solution_text:
$r=0.048/12=0.004$.
The withdrawals form $1400+1400(1.004)+\cdots+1400(1.004)^{n-1}$, with common ratio $1.004$.
$A_n=120000(1.004)^n-\dfrac{1400(1.004^n-1)}{0.004}$.
Setting $A_n=0$ gives $230000(1.004)^n=350000$.
$n=\dfrac{\ln(35/23)}{\ln1.004}$, which lies between $104$ and $105$.
$A_{104}>0$ and $A_{105}<0$, so $104$ complete withdrawals are affordable and month $105$ allows only a partial withdrawal. Ignoring interest gives $85$ complete withdrawals; incorrectly replacing the logarithm's base by $1.048$ gives a value between $8$ and $9$. Exactly one option is correct.
